Figure 1:Comparison of transition modeling paradigms in vision–language–action policies.
(a) Direct VLA maps observations and instructions directly to actions. (b) Reasoning VLA
describes task plans and subgoals in language space. (c) WAM predicts future visual states,
while (d) Latent-WAM predicts future latent representations. (e) VLA-Δ\Deltamodels physical
state changes through multilevel supervision.

Figure 2:Overall architecture of VLA-Δ\Delta. Given multi-view observations, a task instruction, and the robot state,
the model jointly learns a physical state transition representation from Structured Transition Slots,
Optical Flow, and Future-State Difference Text supervision, and uses these representations to condition continuous action generation.
The right panel illustrates the attention-visibility constraints among the different information streams.
Figure 3:Physical state-transition annotations and the automated data annotation pipeline.

Figure 5:Real-robot evaluation on the AgileX PiPER 6-DoF platform. (a) Dual-arm robot
platform. (b) Real-robot experimental results (Success Rates, %). (c) Overview of the five
tasks.
Figure 6:t-SNE visualization of Slot Query hidden states.
